chief_complaint: worsening shortness of breath and productive cough for 5 days
hpi_details: baseline dyspnoea (GOLD 2 COPD), acutely worse over 5 days, increased sputum (yellow-green, increased volume), low-grade fever 37.8°C, no haemoptysis, using rescue inhaler every 2 hours
ideas: thinks it is another chest infection like he gets every winter
concerns: worried he might need to go to hospital as he lives alone
expectations: wants antibiotics and something to help him breathe
pmh: COPD diagnosed 5 years ago, previous smoker, no hospitalisation for COPD in 2 years
medications: tiotropium 18mcg OD, salmeterol/fluticasone 50/500mcg BD, salbutamol 100mcg PRN
social_hx: ex-smoker (quit 5 years ago, 40 pack-years), retired plumber, lives alone, no pets

core_concepts: A COPD exacerbation is an acute worsening of respiratory symptoms, but pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, and acute heart failure can mimic or aggravate it.
If the patient is hypoxemic, oxygen should be controlled and the response monitored rather than given without a target or reassessment.
Short-acting bronchodilators and a short course of systemic corticosteroid are common treatments; antibiotics are selected for clinical indications rather than every exacerbation automatically.
Increased work of breathing or impaired gas exchange should prompt assessment for ventilatory support, including non-invasive ventilation when appropriate.
diagnostic_clues: Known COPD with worsening breathlessness, cough, and sputum
Features suggesting an infective trigger while still requiring assessment for mimics
common_misconceptions: More oxygen is not always better in a patient at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.
Purulent sputum does not remove the need to assess severity and alternative diagnoses.
Antibiotics are not automatic for every COPD exacerbation.
dangerous_errors: Giving uncontrolled oxygen without monitoring in a patient at risk of carbon-dioxide retention
Missing impending ventilatory failure or delaying escalation despite worsening work of breathing
Assuming all acute breathlessness in COPD is an exacerbation and ignoring a dangerous mimic
management_principles: Assess severity, oxygenation, work of breathing, gas exchange, comorbidities, and need for hospital monitoring.
Use controlled oxygen when hypoxemic and reassess with appropriate clinical and laboratory measurements.
Use bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics, and ventilatory support according to severity and clinical indications.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Exact oxygen targets, antibiotic selection, steroid regimen, and admission criteria depend on blood gases, comorbidities, allergies, local resistance, and local protocol.
A patient without hypoxemia does not receive oxygen solely because COPD is present.

source_refs.title: Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease 2026 Report

reference_soap.subjective: 65M with known COPD, 5-day acute exacerbation with increased dyspnoea, purulent sputum, and low-grade fever. Using rescue inhaler Q2h.
reference_soap.objective: O2 saturation, RR, HR, CXR, FEV1 if able, sputum culture, ABG if severe, FBC, CRP.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD), likely infective trigger. DDx: pneumonia, pneumothorax, PE, decompensated heart failure.
reference_soap.plan: Urgently assess severity and need for hospital monitoring. If hypoxemic, provide clinician-directed controlled oxygen with a documented target and reassessment; use bronchodilators and consider systemic corticosteroids or antibiotics only when clinically indicated after examination, blood gases, imaging, and local guidance. Escalate promptly for respiratory distress, worsening gas exchange, or concern for pneumonia, PE, pneumothorax, or cardiac ischemia.

learning_objectives: Assess AECOPD severity using clinical markers
Distinguish AECOPD from pneumonia, PE, cardiac failure
Incorporate social circumstances into management plan

teaching.one_liner: Acute worsening of respiratory symptoms beyond normal day-to-day variations in a patient with underlying COPD, triggered by infection or air pollution.
red_flags: Use of accessory muscles at rest or severe breathlessness at rest
New chest pain, syncope, haemoptysis, unilateral leg swelling, or sudden deterioration suggesting PE, ACS, pneumothorax, or another emergency

must_ask.objective: Anthonisen criteria - Sputum purulence and volume
must_ask.say: Have you noticed your phlegm becoming thicker, greener, or increasing in amount?
Are you getting short of breath even while resting or propping up on extra pillows at night?
Is your quick-relief salbutamol inhaler working as well as usual or failing to give relief?
How many packs of cigarettes did you smoke per day and for how long?
Have you ever been admitted to the ICU or placed on a breathing machine for your lungs?
